lesson.title: From Bobbin Boy to Steel King: Andrew Carnegie's American Rise
lesson.summary: Andrew Carnegie rose from a poor Scottish immigrant to build the dominant American steel company through relentless vertical integration, then gave away most of his fortune, embodying both sides of the robber baron debate.
lesson.body:
Andrew Carnegie was born in 1835 in Dunfermline, Scotland, to a family of handloom weavers whose livelihood was destroyed by industrial competition. In 1848, when Carnegie was thirteen, his family immigrated to the United States and settled near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, then emerging as a center of American iron and steel production. Carnegie started working as a bobbin boy in a textile mill, then moved into telegraph work, catching the attention of Thomas Scott, an executive at the Pennsylvania Railroad. Under Scott's mentorship, Carnegie rose quickly through the railroad's management, learning the operational and financial skills he would later apply to the steel business.

In the 1870s, Carnegie shifted his focus fully to steel, drawn by the enormous demand created by railroad expansion for rails, bridges, and later structural steel for buildings. He invested early in the Bessemer process, a method for converting iron into steel quickly and cheaply, and built the Edgar Thomson Steel Works near Pittsburgh. Carnegie's central strategy was vertical integration, meaning he sought to own or control every stage of steel production himself rather than depend on outside suppliers. His company acquired iron ore fields, including rights in Minnesota's Mesabi Range, coal and coke fields in Pennsylvania, the railroads and ships needed to move raw materials, and the mills that turned it all into finished steel. This let Carnegie Steel cut costs at every step and consistently undercut competitors on price.

Carnegie's business success came with a harsher side. In 1892, workers at the Homestead steel plant near Pittsburgh went on strike after the company, run in Carnegie's absence by his partner Henry Clay Frick, moved to cut wages and break the steelworkers' union. Frick brought in armed Pinkerton detectives to protect strikebreakers, leading to a violent confrontation that left several people dead on both sides. Carnegie, who was in Scotland at the time, publicly supported Frick's hard line afterward, a decision that damaged his reputation among workers and reformers despite his public image as a friend of the working man.

In 1901, Carnegie sold Carnegie Steel to the financier J.P. Morgan for roughly 480 million dollars. Morgan combined it with other steel companies to form United States Steel, the first billion dollar corporation in American history. The sale made Carnegie, briefly, the wealthiest private individual in the world.

Carnegie spent much of his remaining years giving away his fortune, guided by ideas he had laid out in an 1889 essay often called the Gospel of Wealth. In it, he argued that the rich had a moral duty to use their fortunes during their own lifetimes for the public good rather than simply passing wealth to their heirs. He funded the construction of more than 2,500 public libraries across the English speaking world, endowed institutions that still bear his name, and helped establish organizations promoting international peace. Carnegie died in 1919, having given away the great majority of his enormous fortune, leaving behind a legacy that captures both the ruthless competitiveness and the genuine philanthropic ambition of the Gilded Age's leading industrialists.
